name: Metrocable
question: Why is this cable car part of the metro?
clue: Look at how steeply the streets climb below the cabins.
choices: To bypass steep streets and connect hillside neighborhoods
To move goods from warehouses to markets
To link mountain resorts to each other
explanation: Cable cars can climb directly above steep, winding streets. At Acevedo, riders can transfer between the hillside Metrocable and the metro line along the valley.

name: Benthemplein water square
question: Why does this court sit below the surrounding streets?
clue: Notice the steps around the court and the channels leading down to it.
choices: To keep play sheltered from wind
To store stormwater during heavy rain
To make room for underground seating
explanation: Rainwater from the surrounding area flows into sunken basins, including the sports court. The square holds the water temporarily, easing pressure on drainage. When it’s dry, people can play and gather there.

name: Portico of San Luca
question: Why is this uphill walk covered for so much of the route?
clue: The arches continue up the hill, following the path.
choices: To mark where the city walls once stood
To carry drinking water uphill
To shelter people walking to a hilltop sanctuary
explanation: The long portico shelters people walking to the Sanctuary of San Luca. It takes the covered walkway familiar in Bologna’s streets and carries it up a hill, where shade and protection from rain make a difference on a long walk.

name: Stationsplein bicycle parking
question: Why put thousands of bike spaces beneath the water here?
clue: This bicycle garage is directly beside Amsterdam Centraal.
choices: To store bikes awaiting export by boat
To free up surface space and make bike-to-train transfers easy
To move rental bikes away from the city centre
explanation: Cyclists can leave their bikes near the station and continue by train. Putting the garage under the water makes room for thousands of bikes while freeing space on the busy surface around the station.

name: Central–Mid-Levels escalator
question: Why does this hillside escalator switch direction during the day?
clue: The route links hillside homes with the business district below.
choices: To follow the direction of the morning commute
To match the direction of traffic on nearby streets
To alternate access to two different hillside neighborhoods
explanation: In the morning, the escalator carries people downhill toward Central. Later it runs uphill, making the climb back toward Mid-Levels easier. The same infrastructure serves two different flows over the course of a day.

name: Acqua alta walkways
question: Why does Venice set up these raised walkways?
clue: Look at where the boards sit relative to the water around them.
choices: To protect fragile paving from crowds
To keep people walking during high water
To create separate queues for boats
explanation: Temporary walkways keep selected pedestrian routes usable when high tides flood low streets and squares. The city sets out the platforms along planned routes according to expected water levels.

name: Bishan–Ang Mo Kio Park
question: Why replace a straight concrete canal with a winding river in a park?
clue: Notice how much open space there is between the water and the paths.
choices: To give high flows room to spread
To create a shorter route for water
To keep the river at a fixed width
explanation: The landscaped banks give the river room to expand during heavy rain. At lower flows, the same corridor provides space for park users and habitats along the water.

name: Tube bus stations
question: Why do people wait inside a raised tube before boarding?
clue: Compare the platform height with the floor of a bus.
choices: To keep passengers above seasonal floodwater
To give buses a covered place to park
To collect fares before boarding and let people board at floor level
explanation: Riders pay at the station and wait on a raised platform. When the bus arrives, passengers can board near floor level, so less time is spent collecting fares and climbing steps at the door.

name: Thames Barrier
question: Why do these structures leave gaps across the river?
clue: Look at the openings between the piers.
choices: To let ships through while gates are lowered
To funnel fast water through turbines
To separate river traffic into fixed lanes
explanation: The gates usually rest below the river surface so boats can pass. When a dangerous surge is forecast, the gates can rotate up between the piers to help protect London from flooding.

name: RÉSO pedestrian network
question: Why connect buildings with passages below the street?
clue: The corridor leads toward several destinations without reaching an outdoor crossing.
choices: To keep walking routes open while linking transit, shops and offices
To reserve the passages for building deliveries
To replace street-level bus routes with tunnels
explanation: The RÉSO links parts of downtown, including métro stations, shops and offices. Its indoor passages let pedestrians make many everyday trips while sheltered from snow and cold.

name: Cheonggyecheon
question: Why did Seoul remove a highway to bring this stream back into view?
clue: Look at the walking paths below the surrounding streets.
choices: To make a shipping channel
To reconnect downtown with a public stream corridor
To extend the road network below ground
explanation: The city removed the elevated road and opened up the stream corridor. Paths, crossings and planted banks turned the space into a public route through downtown.

name: Eixample street corners
question: Why are the corners of these blocks clipped?
clue: Look for the extra space where four blocks meet.
choices: To make intersections wider and easier to see across
To mark the old city gates
To make every block face south
explanation: The Eixample plan cut back the corners of its blocks. The chamfers give people and vehicles more room at intersections and open views along the crossing streets.

name: Abandoibarra waterfront
question: Why place a major museum beside this river?
clue: Look at the open riverbank around the museum.
choices: To use the river for shipping exhibits
To protect the city from high tides
To draw people back to a former industrial waterfront
explanation: The Guggenheim was part of a broader redevelopment of a former port and industrial area. Public paths and spaces made the riverbank a place to visit and walk through.

name: Chicago River
question: Why did Chicago engineer this river to flow away from Lake Michigan?
clue: The river runs through the city beside the lake that supplies its drinking water.
choices: To keep sewage away from the drinking-water intake
To turn the river into a reservoir
To stop boats entering the city
explanation: Chicago opened a canal that redirected the river toward the Mississippi basin. The aim was to keep sewage carried by the river from reaching the city’s drinking-water supply in Lake Michigan.

name: Lake Burley Griffin
question: Why create a lake between parts of the capital?
clue: Look at how the bridge spans a broad body of water through the city.
choices: To serve as an ocean shipping terminal
To anchor the capital’s layout around a central landscape
To remove the need for bridges
explanation: The capital plan used a lake as a central feature, relating the city’s layout to the valley and surrounding hills. Damming the Molonglo River created the lake and bridges connected the two sides.

name: Ringstrasse
question: Why does a broad boulevard loop around Vienna’s old centre?
clue: The opera house stands along the edge of the old core.
choices: To mark the banks of a filled-in river
To follow the route of an old railway
To reuse the space occupied by the city’s defences
explanation: Vienna replaced its old fortifications with the Ringstrasse. The boulevard and the ground around it made room for civic and cultural buildings, including the opera house.

name: Royal Crescent
question: Why make this row of houses look like one building?
clue: Look for the repeating columns and uninterrupted curve.
choices: To give separate homes a unified frontage
To create one large indoor market
To support a wall around the city
explanation: The Royal Crescent uses a coordinated façade across separate homes. The curve and repeating columns make the street read as a single architectural composition.
credit: Photographed by Adrian Pingstone on April 20th 2005 and placed in the public domain.

name: Perret’s rebuilt centre
question: Why do so many buildings around this square repeat the same spacing?
clue: Look for regular intervals between columns and windows.
choices: To disguise houses built in different centuries
To rebuild the centre using a shared construction system
To follow the bends of a former river
explanation: After wartime destruction, Auguste Perret’s team used a shared modular grid and reinforced concrete. The repeated dimensions helped coordinate construction across the rebuilt centre.

name: Dejima
question: Why is the outline of an old island visible inside the modern city?
clue: Look for the fan shape surrounded by today’s streets.
choices: A bridge collapsed and left it stranded
The island drifted toward shore
Land reclamation filled in the water around it
explanation: Dejima was an artificial island used to control contact and trade with foreign merchants. As Nagasaki reclaimed land from the harbour, the island became part of the mainland street fabric.

name: Granary Island
question: Why did this waterfront island become a place to store grain?
clue: Look at how closely the buildings face the water.
choices: Bulk cargo could move between warehouses and boats
The grain had to be grown on the island
The island was the only place protected from wind
explanation: Gdańsk exported grain through its port. Warehouses on the Motława kept large stocks near the vessels that moved them. The photo shows later development on that historic site.

name: Pingjiang Road
question: Why do a street and a canal run side by side here?
clue: Notice how buildings and crossings serve both the lane and the water.
choices: The canal was an unused building trench
The neighbourhood developed around routes on foot and by boat
The canal was dug to keep pedestrians off the street
explanation: Suzhou’s historic neighbourhoods grew around parallel land and water routes. The canal provided a way to move by boat, while the street and bridges linked nearby buildings on foot.

name: Royal Albert Dock
question: Why build warehouses right at the edge of this dock?
clue: The warehouse fronts rise straight above the basin.
choices: To keep ships outside the port
To create a barrier against ocean waves
To unload goods straight from ships into storage
explanation: Ships could unload directly into the Albert Dock warehouses, reducing transfers on land. Brick, stone and iron also reduced the fire risk associated with timber construction.

name: Stari Most
question: Why use one broad arch over this river?
clue: Notice that the bridge meets the banks without a pier in the channel.
choices: To cross the river without a support in the water
To hold water behind the bridge
To carry boats over the valley
explanation: The stone arch carries the crossing between the banks in a single span. The bridge joins the two sides of the old town over the deep Neretva channel.

name: Janganmun gate
question: Why put a substantial gate where a road passes through the city wall?
clue: Look at the opening and the structure above it.
choices: To keep the road open in every direction
To control access while keeping a route through the fortress
To carry water over the road
explanation: The fortress wall needed gateways for people and traffic. A defended gate let the city control entry at a point where the road interrupted the wall.

name: Atomic Bomb Dome
question: Why preserve this damaged building in the centre of Hiroshima?
clue: Look at the exposed frame and brickwork that survived.
choices: To finish it later as an exhibition hall
To demonstrate a new type of construction
To keep a visible record of the bombing and its human cost
explanation: Hiroshima preserved the surviving structure as part of its peace memorial. The building’s condition makes the destruction visible and gives the surrounding memorial landscape a physical point of remembrance.

name: Colosseum
question: How could crowds reach so many seats quickly?
clue: Notice the repeated arches around the outside.
choices: Many entrances fed separate stairs and corridors
Spectators climbed ladders from the arena
Everyone used a single central ramp
explanation: The outer arches led into a network of corridors and stairs. Distributing arrivals around the perimeter helped spectators reach their sections without funneling everyone through one gate.

name: Gion street fronts
question: Why do many of these buildings have narrow fronts along the street?
clue: Look at how closely the entrances sit next to one another.
choices: They were designed as detached houses with side gardens
Long, narrow plots gave many properties direct street access
The façades were temporary screens for festivals
explanation: Kyoto’s traditional townhouses often occupy narrow plots that extend back from the street. That arrangement puts many entrances and shopfronts along a block, with more living and working space behind them.

name: Dubai Creek
question: Why did merchants set up along this creek?
clue: Look at how boats can reach buildings deep inland from the coast.
choices: The creek had no connection to the sea
The banks blocked trade between neighborhoods
The inlet gave boats a sheltered route to markets
explanation: Dubai Creek brought maritime traffic inland to markets and wharves. Boats could unload goods close to traders, making the banks a working commercial corridor.

name: The planned capital
question: Why does the capital put major civic buildings along a broad axis?
clue: Look at the generous open spaces around the public buildings.
choices: To organize national institutions along a clear civic spine
To trace a former railway line
To fit the streets between steep ravines
explanation: Lúcio Costa’s plan used a monumental axis for major government and civic buildings. A separate axis organizes much of the residential fabric, giving different functions distinct places in the plan.

name: The fortified peninsula
question: Why do fortifications wrap around this narrow city?
clue: Notice the water on both sides of the built-up ridge.
choices: To keep the sea away from freshwater farms
To defend the peninsula and its harbour approaches
To provide a raised promenade above a railway
explanation: Valletta occupies a peninsula between two harbours. Fortifications around its edges helped defend the city and the waters on either side, while a street grid organized the interior.

name: Stone Town
question: Why does this port neighbourhood contain so many architectural traditions?
clue: Look at the doors, balconies and street fronts built close together.
choices: Its buildings were imported intact from Europe
It was laid out as a single modern housing project
Indian Ocean trade brought people and building traditions together
explanation: Stone Town was a trading centre where African, Arab, Indian and European influences met. Craftspeople and residents brought those influences into details such as carved doors and street-facing balconies.
credit: No machine-readable author provided. Mbz1 assumed (based on copyright claims).

name: Avenue de l’Opéra
question: Why cut a straight avenue through an older street network?
clue: Look down the clear line of sight toward the opera house.
choices: To connect important destinations and create a direct vista
To follow the edge of a canal
To fit the street around a surviving city wall
explanation: The avenue created a direct route toward the opera and a prominent view of its façade. It was part of a period of major street rebuilding that changed how people moved through central Paris.

name: Art Deco streets
question: Why do neighbouring buildings share a style from the same era?
clue: Look for the repeated geometric decoration along the street.
choices: An earthquake led to much of the centre being rebuilt at once
The buildings were relocated from a film set
A port warehouse was divided into all of the shops
explanation: The 1931 earthquake and fires devastated central Napier. Much of the rebuilding happened in the years that followed, so many buildings reflect architectural fashions of the same period, including Art Deco.

name: Capitol Complex
question: Why group these large public buildings in one precinct?
clue: Notice how the buildings share open ground instead of lining a shopping street.
choices: To consolidate wholesale markets
To set out the institutions of a planned capital together
To turn the site into a residential superblock
explanation: Chandigarh’s Capitol Complex groups the assembly, secretariat and high court. The shared precinct gives the main institutions of government a deliberate place in the plan of the new capital.

name: Boott Cotton Mills
question: Why are the former mills clustered near the river?
clue: Look at how the industrial buildings sit along the water.
choices: To move finished buildings downriver
To irrigate fields in the mill yards
To draw power from water routed through canals
explanation: Lowell’s canals distributed water from the Merrimack River to textile mills. The flow drove machinery, making access to the canal system important to where the mills were built.

name: The Peristyle
question: Why is a Roman palace courtyard now part of the city’s street life?
clue: Look at how later buildings meet the ancient columns.
choices: A new park copied an ancient courtyard
Residents adapted the palace precinct into a living town
The whole courtyard was moved from the countryside
explanation: After the Roman period, people lived and built within the former palace. Streets and buildings grew around surviving structures, and the Peristyle became part of the occupied city.

name: The Sassi
question: How could homes be built into a steep ravine?
clue: Notice the buildings stacked against the slope.
choices: Builders cut rooms into the rock and added masonry fronts
Builders levelled the entire ravine before construction
Each home was built on a floating platform
explanation: Many dwellings combine spaces cut into soft rock with built façades and additions. Paths, roofs and stairs fit together at different levels of the slope.
credit: No machine-readable author provided. Atigra~commonswiki assumed (based on copyright claims).

name: Pombaline Baixa
question: Why does this older city have such a regular downtown grid?
clue: Look for the straight streets and repeating blocks.
choices: The grid follows Roman farm boundaries exactly
The centre was rebuilt to a coordinated plan after an earthquake
The streets were once parallel rivers
explanation: After the 1755 earthquake, planners laid out the lower city with straighter streets and regular blocks. Coordinated building designs made it possible to reconstruct whole streets together.

name: The hills above the port
question: Why did this port develop lifts up its hillsides?
clue: Look at the steep rise immediately behind the waterfront.
choices: To lower ships into the harbour
To move cargo between offshore vessels
To connect hillside homes with streets below
explanation: The flat land near the port is narrow and much of the city climbs the hills. Inclined lifts helped connect higher neighbourhoods with the lower streets and waterfront.

name: Trading streets
question: Why did merchants build so close to the waterfront?
clue: Look at the compact row of buildings beside the river.
choices: The river linked trading houses with boats carrying goods
The waterfront was reserved for farming
Merchants needed to be as far as possible from the port
explanation: Hội An grew as a trading port on the Thu Bồn River. Streets, houses and wharves formed a compact district where merchants could receive, store and exchange goods close to boat traffic.

name: Såheim power station
question: Why put a large power station in this mountain valley?
clue: Look at the steep slopes behind the building.
choices: To use tides to turn turbines
To use water falling from higher ground
To burn coal brought in by ocean ships
explanation: Water descending from the surrounding high ground could drive turbines. Hydroelectric power supported energy-intensive industrial production in a valley far from a major coastal port.

name: Salts Mill
question: Why build a mill village beside a canal and railway?
clue: Look at how the large mill sits within a compact settlement.
choices: The canal supplied seawater for the machinery
The railway separated the mill from all housing
The links moved supplies and goods while workers lived nearby
explanation: The mill stood close to canal and rail transport, which helped move materials and products. Housing and services nearby tied the settlement to the daily needs of the workforce.
credit: No machine-readable author provided. Jungpionier assumed (based on copyright claims).

name: Chain Bridge
question: What did a permanent bridge change for the two sides of the Danube?
clue: Notice the wide gap the crossing spans.
choices: People and goods could cross without depending on ferries or seasonal crossings
Ships no longer needed the river
The two banks became separate port districts
explanation: The Chain Bridge created a permanent crossing between Buda and Pest. More dependable movement across the river helped the two sides function as parts of one city.

name: San Felipe de Barajas fortress
question: Why put this fortress on a hill overlooking the approaches?
clue: Look at how the walls rise above the surrounding ground.
choices: To collect water in a valley reservoir
To oversee and defend routes into the port city
To create a sheltered dock for ships
explanation: The fortress occupies high ground outside the historic centre. From there defenders could oversee approaches on land and reinforce the wider system protecting the port.

name: Upper and Lower Town
question: Why did the old city develop on two levels?
clue: Look at the drop between the bluff and the riverfront.
choices: A canal once ran along the top of the cliff
The upper streets were built to load ships
The bluff served defence while the riverfront served trade
explanation: The heights above the St. Lawrence offered a defensive position. The lower town grew near the water, where ships landed and merchants traded.

name: The city walls
question: Why carry the walls along the coast as well as around the land side?
clue: Look at how tightly the fortifications follow the town’s edge.
choices: The maritime city needed defences against approaches by sea and land
The walls marked the limits of a farming estate
The walls channelled a river through the town
explanation: Dubrovnik’s prosperity depended on maritime trade. Walls and forts enclosed the town and helped protect the harbour and the approaches from both the sea and inland.

name: Old and New Towns
question: Why do two adjoining districts have such different street patterns?
clue: Compare the ridge of the Old Town with the more regular streets beyond it.
choices: The two districts were once on separate islands
A planned expansion added a regular layout beside a medieval ridge town
The grid was laid out as a railway yard
explanation: The Old Town followed a ridge with narrow routes branching off it. The later New Town was planned on different ground, using broad streets and regular blocks.

name: Sydney Harbour Bridge
question: Why span the harbour with a large arch?
clue: Look at the clear waterway below the road and rail deck.
choices: To give sailing ships a platform for unloading
To divide the harbour into separate reservoirs
To carry heavy traffic while leaving room for vessels below
explanation: The steel arch supports a deck for road and rail traffic. The broad span keeps major supports out of the shipping channel and gives vessels clearance beneath the crossing.

name: The reclaimed waterfront
question: Why is part of the city centre on land that used to be water?
clue: Notice the broad, built-up edge beside the working harbour.
choices: Reclamation made room for wharves and land-side port activity
A river changed course and exposed its bed overnight
The land was raised solely to build a sea wall
explanation: Auckland extended parts of its shoreline by filling in shallow areas. Reclaimed ground gave the growing port more space for wharves, freight and streets connecting the waterfront to the city.

name: Old Port
question: Why did the old port grow around this long inlet?
clue: Look at how the water reaches into the city between two sides of the harbour.
choices: It let boats reach a hilltop market without unloading
The inlet offered sheltered water and long edges for quays
It kept the port isolated from surrounding streets
explanation: The inlet gave vessels shelter from the open Mediterranean and put them close to the city. Quays along the banks turned that natural shape into a working harbour.
